title: Celsus declares but does not teach
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἐν ᾗ ἐξεθέμην τοῦ Κέλσου λέξει παραφραζούσῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ Τιμαίου τινὰ γέγραπται, ὡς ἄρα ὁ μὲν θεὸς οὐδὲν θνητὸν ἐποίησεν ἀλλὰ μόνα τὰ ἀθάνατα, τὰ δὲ θνητὰ ἄλλων ἐστὶν ἔργα. καὶ ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον. σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις. καὶ οὐδὲν διοίσει σῶμα ἀνθρώπου σώματος νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου· ὕλη γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ, καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτῶν ὅμοιον· φέρε καὶ περὶ τούτων ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον διαλάβωμεν, ἐλέγχοντες τὸν ἤτοι μὴ προσποιούμενον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ Ἐπικούρειον γνώμην ἢ, ὡς ἂν εἴποι ἄν τις, ὕστερον μεταθέμενον ἐπὶ τὰ βελτίω ἢ καὶ, ὡς ἂν (ἄλλος τις) λέγοι. τὸν ὁμώνυμον τῷ Ἐπικουρείῳ. τοιαῦτα γὰρ ἐχρῆν αὐτὸν ἀποφαινόμενον καὶ ἐναντία λέγειν οὐ μόνον ἡμῖν προθέμενον ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἀγεννεῖ φιλοσόφων αἱρέσει τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κιτιέως Ζήνωνος κατασκευάσαι ὅτι τὰ τῶν ζῴων σώματα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ. καὶ ὅτι ἡ τοσαύτη περὶ αὐτὰ τέχνη οὐκ ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου ἐλήλυθε νοῦ. ἔδει δ᾿ αὐτὸν καὶ περὶ τῶν τοσούτων καὶ ὑπὸ ἐνυπαρχούσης ἀφαντάστου φύσεως διοικουμένων παντοδαπῶν φυτῶν καὶ πρὸς χρείαν γεγονότων οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητον ἐν τῷ παντὶ ἀνθρώπων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώποις διακονουμένων ζῴων, ὅπως ποτὲ ἄλλως ὄντων, μὴ ἀποφήνασθαι μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ διδάξαι ὅτι μὴ τέλειός τις νοῦς τὰς τοσαύτας ἐνεποίησε ποιότητας τῇ ὕλῃ τῶν φυτῶν. εἰ δ᾿ ἅπαξ θεοὺς ἐποίει δημιουργοὺς πάντων σωμάτων, ὡς μόνης ψυχῆς ἔργον οὔσης θεοῦ, πῶς οὐχὶ ἑξῆς ἦν τῷ μερίζοντι τὰ τοσαῦτα δημιουργήματα καὶ πολλοῖς διδόντι μετά τινος κατασκευάσαι οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτου λόγου θεῶν διαφορὰς. τῶνδε μὲν ἀνθρώπεια κατασκευαζόντων σώματα ἑτέρων δὲ φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν κτήνεια καὶ ἄλλων θήρεια; ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν, ὁρῶντα θεοὺς δρακόντων καὶ ἀσπίδων καὶ βασιλίσκων δημιουργοὺς καὶ κατὰ ἄτομον εἶδος αὐτῶν τινας εἶναι δημιουργοὺς καὶ ἄλλους κατ᾿ εἶδος ἑκάστου φυτοῦ καὶ ἑκάστης βοτάνης, λέγειν τὰς αἰτίας τῶν μερισμῶν. ἴσως γὰρ ἂν ἐπιδοὺς ἑαυτὸν τῇ ἀκριβείᾳ τῆς τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον βασάνου ἤτοι ἐτήρει ἕνα θεὸν πάντων δημιουργὸν, πρός τι καὶ ἕνεκέν τινος ἕκαστον πεποιηκότα, ἢ μὴ τηρῶν ἑώρα τί χρὴ αὐτὸν ἀπολογήσασθαι περὶ ἀδιαφόρου τῇ αὐτοῦ φύσει πράγματος τοῦ φθαρτοῦ, καὶ ὅτι οὐδὲν ἄτοπον τὸν ἐξ ἀνομοίων συνεστηκότα κόσμον ὑπὸ ἑνὸς γεγονέναι τεχνίτου, συμφερόντως τῷ ὅλῳ τὰς διαφορὰς τῶν εἰδῶν κατασκευάζοντος. ἢ τὸ ἔσχατόν γε ἔδει αὐτὸν περὶ τηλικούτου δόγματος μηδ᾿ ἀποφαίνεσθαι τὴν ἀρχὴν, εἴπερ κατασκευάζειν οὐκ ἔμελλεν ἅπερ διδάσκειν ἐπηγγέλλετο· εἰ μὴ ἄρα ὁ ἐγκαλῶν τοῖς ψιλὴν πίστιν ἐπαγγελλομένοις αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς πιστεύειν ἐβούλετο οἷς ἀπεφήνατο, καίτοι γε οὐ τὸ ἀποφήνασθαι ἀλλὰ τὸ διδάξαι ἐπαγγειλάμενος.
pass_a_gloss: Since in the passage (λέξις) of Celsus that I set out (ἐκτίθημι), paraphrasing (παραφράζω) certain things from the Timaeus, it is written that God made (ποιέω) nothing mortal (θνητός) but only the immortal things (ἀθάνατος), and mortal things are works (ἔργον) of others; and soul (ψυχή) is God's work, but of body (σῶμα) another nature (ἄλλη φύσις); and a man's body will differ (διαφέρω, fut. διοίσει) in nothing from the body of a bat (νυκτερίς) or worm/maggot (εὐλή) or frog (βάτραχος); for the matter (ὕλη) is the same and their corruptible (τὸ φθαρτόν) alike (ὅμοιος) — come (φέρε), let us discuss (διαλαμβάνω) these for a little, refuting (ἐλέγχω) the one who either does not profess (προσποιέομαι) his own Epicurean opinion (γνώμη), or, as one might say, later changed over (μετατίθημι) to better things, or even, as another might say, the namesake (ὁμώνυμος) of the Epicurean. For declaring (ἀποφαίνομαι) such things, and having proposed (προτίθημι) to speak against not only us but also the not ignoble (ἀγεννής neg.) school (αἵρεσις) of philosophers from Zeno of Citium, he ought (χρή) to have established (κατασκευάζω) that the bodies of animals (ζῷον) are not works of God, and that the so great craft (τέχνη) about them has not come from the first Mind (πρῶτος νοῦς). He ought also concerning so many plants (φυτόν) of every kind (παντοδαπός), governed (διοικέω) by an indwelling (ἐνυπάρχω) nature without impressions (ἀφάνταστος φύσις), and come to be for a not-despicable use (χρεία) in the universe of men and of animals serving (διακονέω) men, however else they may be, not only to declare but also to teach that no perfect (τέλειος) mind implanted (ἐμποιέω) so many qualities (ποιότης) in the matter of plants. And if once he made gods craftsmen (δημιουργός) of all bodies, as only the soul being God's work, how was it not consistent (ἑξῆς) for the one dividing (μερίζω) so many works of craft (δημιούργημα) and giving them to many to establish with some not-despicable reasoning differences (διαφορά) of gods: these making human bodies, others, say, of cattle (κτήνειος), others of wild beasts (θήρειος)? He ought, seeing gods as craftsmen of serpents (δράκων), asps (ἀσπίς), basilisks (βασιλίσκος), and some craftsmen according to each indivisible species (ἄτομον εἶδος) of them, and others according to the species of each plant and herb (βοτάνη), to state the causes (αἰτία) of the divisions (μερισμός). For perhaps, giving himself (ἐπιδίδωμι) to precision (ἀκρίβεια) of testing (βάσανος) matters on the topic, he would either have kept (τηρέω) one God craftsman of all, having made each thing toward something and for the sake of something, or not keeping it, would have seen what he must defend (ἀπολογέομαι) about the corruptible, a thing indifferent (ἀδιάφορος) in its own nature, and that nothing absurd (ἄτοπος) that the world (κόσμος) composed of unlike things (ἀνόμοιος) came to be from one craftsman (τεχνίτης), fashioning the differences of species advantageously (συμφερόντως) to the whole. Or at last he ought not even at all to declare about so great a doctrine (δόγμα), if he was not going to establish what he professed (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to teach; unless the one accusing (ἐγκαλέω) those professing bare faith (ψιλὴ πίστις) himself wanted us to believe (πιστεύω) what he declared, though having professed not to declare but to teach (διδάσκω).
pass_b_english: In the passage of Celsus that I set out, which paraphrases certain things from the Timaeus (Plato, Timaeus 41a–d), it is written that God made nothing mortal, but only immortal things, while mortal things are the works of others; that “the soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature”; and that a man’s body will differ in nothing from the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog, “for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.” Come, then, let us discuss these points too for a little while. We shall be refuting a man who either does not acknowledge his own Epicurean opinion, or, as someone might say, later changed over to better views, or even, as another might say, is a namesake of the Epicurean.

For in declaring such things, having set out to speak against not only us but also the far from contemptible school of philosophers who follow Zeno of Citium, he ought to have proved that the bodies of living creatures are not works of God, and that the great skill shown in them did not come from the first Mind. So too with the countless plants of every kind, which are governed by an indwelling nature that has no sense-impressions, and which came into being to serve a use of no small account in the universe, for men and for the animals that serve men, whatever else may be true of them: he ought not only to have declared but also to have taught that it was not some perfect mind that implanted so many qualities in the matter of plants.

And if once he made gods the craftsmen of all bodies, on the ground that the soul alone is God’s work, how would it not have been consistent for one who divides up so many works of craft and assigns them to many to establish, with some argument of real weight, differences among the gods: some fashioning the bodies of men, others, let us say, those of cattle, and others those of wild beasts? Seeing gods as the craftsmen of serpents and asps and basilisks, some of them makers of each particular species of these, and others makers of the species of each plant and each herb, he ought to have stated the reasons for these divisions. For perhaps, had he given himself to examining the questions of this topic with precision, he would either have held to one God, the Maker of all, who made each thing for some end and for the sake of something; or, if he did not hold to this, he would have seen what defence he must make about the perishable, a thing indifferent in its own nature, and that there is nothing absurd in a world composed of unlike things having come into being from one Craftsman, who fashions the differences of species for the good of the whole.

Or at the very least he ought not to have pronounced on so great a doctrine at all, if he was not going to prove what he professed to teach. Unless, perhaps, the man who blames those who profess bare faith wanted us ourselves to believe what he declared, even though what he professed was not to declare but to teach.

Origen reports Celsus here with ὡς ἄρα; only the two clauses that match the wording of Celsus in 4.52 verbatim (ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον, σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις; ὕλη γὰρ ἡ αὐτή, καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτῶν ὅμοιον) are put in quotation marks; the rest is Origen's restatement and is left unquoted. Timaeus reference: the Demiurge makes the immortal part and hands the mortal to the younger gods (Timaeus 41a–d; compare 69c). Koetschau's supplied ⟨ἄλλος τις⟩ (shown as '(ἄλλος τις)' in the staged text) is followed. ἀφάνταστος φύσις is the Stoic term for the 'nature' that governs plants, which lack sense-impression (φαντασία), rendered 'an indwelling nature that has no sense-impressions'. ὅπως ποτὲ ἄλλως ὄντων is taken as a concession ('whatever else may be true of them'). ἄτομον εἶδος (the lowest, indivisible species) is rendered 'each particular species'. 'first Mind' (πρῶτος νοῦς) is capitalised as it names God; τέλειός τις νοῦς is indefinite and left lowercase. The final 'promised ... to teach' points back to Celsus's ἐθέλω διδάξαι in 4.52. No Scripture in this chapter.
